title: Web Development Foundations
description: Go from a blank page to a working, responsive site — structure, style, interactivity, and getting it online.

modules.title: HTML Basics
modules.body: Structure a page with semantic tags, understand the document tree, and build your first real markup by hand.
modules.intro: HTML gives a web page its structure — it's the skeleton everything else (CSS, JavaScript) hangs off of. Every element you place on a page, from a heading to an image, is an HTML tag, and the way tags nest inside one another forms a tree the browser reads to decide what to draw and in what order.
core:
Tags come in pairs that wrap content, like

...

for a paragraph or

...

for a top-level heading; a few, like and
, are self-closing.
Semantic elements — <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <footer> — describe what a section of the page *means*, not just how it looks. Screen readers and search engines both rely on this meaning.
Attributes add extra information to a tag: href on a link, src and alt on an image, class or id for styling and scripting hooks.
Nesting tags inside each other builds the Document Object Model (DOM) — a tree structure that CSS and JavaScript both use to find and style specific parts of the page.
modules.example:
My First Post

Welcome to my new blog.
modules.exercise:
Build a single HTML file for a short personal bio: one

with your name, a

introducing yourself, an (any placeholder image URL works), and an link to a site you like. Open it in a browser and check that everything appears in the order you expect.

modules.title: CSS Layouts
modules.body: Use flexbox and grid to arrange page elements, and learn the box model that everything else builds on.
modules.intro: CSS controls how HTML looks and where things sit on the page. Before touching layout, it helps to understand the box model: every element is a rectangular box made of content, padding, a border, and a margin, stacked from the inside out.
core: The box model: padding sits inside the border (space around your content), margin sits outside it (space between elements). box-sizing: border-box makes width/height include padding and border, which is usually what you want.
Flexbox (display: flex) is built for one-dimensional layouts — a row or a column of items. justify-content controls spacing along the main axis, align-items controls the cross axis.
CSS Grid (display: grid) is built for two-dimensional layouts — rows and columns at once. grid-template-columns defines the column widths directly.
Rule of thumb: reach for flexbox when arranging items in a line, grid when you're laying out a whole page or a card grid.
modules.exercise: Build a row of three equal-width "cards" using flexbox, each with a heading and a short paragraph, evenly spaced with a gap between them. Then try converting the same layout to CSS grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) and compare how much CSS each approach needed.

modules.title: JavaScript Essentials
modules.body: Variables, functions, and events — enough JavaScript to make a page respond to what someone does on it.
modules.intro: JavaScript is what turns a static page into something interactive. At its core, it's about storing values in variables, packaging logic into functions, and reacting to events like clicks or keystrokes.
core: let declares a variable that can be reassigned later; const declares one that can't. Prefer const by default and switch to let only when you know a value will change.
A function packages up a piece of logic so you can reuse it: function greet(name) { return "Hi " + name; } or the shorter arrow form const greet = (name) => "Hi " + name;.
document.querySelector('.btn') finds an element on the page; addEventListener('click', fn) tells the browser to run fn whenever that element is clicked.
Reading an error message from the bottom up (the actual error) before the top (the call stack) usually gets you to the real problem faster.
modules.exercise: Add a button to an HTML page that toggles a paragraph's text between two states when clicked (e.g. "Show details" / "Hide details"). Then extend it so a second click brings back the original state.

modules.title: Responsive Design
modules.body: Write CSS that adapts to any screen, from a phone to a wide monitor, using breakpoints and relative units.
modules.intro: A responsive site rearranges itself to stay usable whether it's viewed on a phone or a wide desktop monitor. The common strategy is to design for the smallest screen first, then add complexity as space allows.
core: Mobile-first CSS starts with simple, stacked styles for narrow screens, then uses media queries to add multi-column layouts as the viewport grows — this tends to produce simpler, more maintainable CSS than the reverse.
A media query like @media (min-width: 768px) { ... } applies styles only above a given screen width, called a breakpoint.
Relative units — %, rem, vw — scale with their context or the viewport, unlike fixed px values, which is why they're preferred for widths and font sizes in responsive layouts.
Images should have max-width: 100% so they shrink to fit their container instead of overflowing it.
modules.exercise: Take the three-card layout from the CSS Layouts module and make it stack vertically below 600px wide, then switch to a horizontal row above that. Resize your browser window to test both states.

modules.title: Forms & Validation
modules.body: Collect input safely: build forms, validate them in the browser, and give clear feedback on errors.
modules.intro: Forms are how a page collects information from a visitor — a signup, a search box, a checkout. Getting validation right means catching obvious mistakes early without being annoying about it.
core: HTML input types do a lot of validation for free: type="email" checks for an @ sign, type="number" restricts to digits, and the required attribute blocks empty submission.
The pattern attribute lets you enforce a custom format with a regular expression when built-in types aren't specific enough.
The :invalid CSS pseudo-class lets you style a field differently the moment its value doesn't pass validation, which is useful for real-time feedback.
Client-side validation is about user experience, not security — a malicious user can bypass it entirely, so the server must always re-validate anything it receives.
modules.exercise: Build a small signup form with a name field (required), an email field (type="email", required), and a password field (minlength="8"). Try submitting it empty and with an invalid email to see the browser's built-in error messages.

modules.title: Deploying Your Site
modules.body: Take a finished project from your machine to a live URL that anyone can open.
modules.intro: A finished project sitting on your laptop isn't a website yet — deploying it means putting the files somewhere the public internet can reach, at a stable address.
core: A build step compiles your source files (which might use tools like Sass or a framework) into plain HTML/CSS/JS that any browser can run.
Static hosts — GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel — are built specifically for front-end-only sites: you push your files, and they're served from a URL within minutes, usually for free.
A custom domain is really just a DNS record pointing a name you own (like yoursite.com) at your host's servers; it's a configuration step, not a rebuild.
Your local dev server (e.g. localhost:3000) is only reachable from your own machine — deployment is what makes the same project reachable from anywhere.
modules.example:
# A typical static deploy, using the Netlify CLI
netlify deploy --prod --dir=./build
modules.exercise: Take any small HTML/CSS project you've built and deploy it to a free static host of your choice. Confirm you can open the live URL from a different device (like your phone) to prove it's really public.

title: Data Science Starter
description: Load real data, clean it, look at it from a few angles, and pull out a finding worth sharing.

modules.title: Python Basics
modules.body: The core syntax you need before touching a dataset: lists, loops, functions, and reading error messages.
modules.intro: Python is the most common language for data work because its syntax stays out of the way. Before loading any real data, it helps to be comfortable with a handful of core building blocks.
core: A list holds an ordered collection: scores = [88, 92, 79]. A dictionary holds key-value pairs: student = {"name": "Ana", "score": 88}.
A for loop repeats an action across a collection: for score in scores: print(score).
A function packages logic for reuse: def average(nums): return sum(nums) / len(nums).
Reading a Python traceback from the bottom up shows you the actual error first (e.g. TypeError, KeyError) before the chain of calls that led to it.
modules.exercise: Write a function that takes a list of numbers and returns the highest and lowest values as a tuple. Test it on a list you make up, including one with negative numbers.

modules.title: Data with Pandas
modules.body: Load a spreadsheet into Python, filter and reshape it, and handle the missing values that show up.
modules.intro: pandas is the standard Python library for working with tabular data — the kind you'd otherwise put in a spreadsheet. Its core object, the DataFrame, represents a table with labeled rows and columns.
core: pd.read_csv("file.csv") loads a spreadsheet into a DataFrame in one line.
Filtering rows uses a boolean condition: df[df["age"] > 30]. Selecting columns uses their names: df[["name", "age"]].
Missing values show up as NaN. df.dropna() removes rows with any missing values; df.fillna(0) replaces them with a chosen value — which one you pick depends on what the missing value actually means.
df.groupby("category").mean() is one of the most common patterns: split the data into groups, then summarize each group.
modules.example:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df = df.dropna(subset=["revenue"])
print(df.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum())
modules.exercise: Find any small CSV file (or make one with 10-20 rows in a spreadsheet and export it), load it with pandas, and print the average of one numeric column grouped by one categorical column.

modules.title: Visualizing Data
modules.body: Turn a table of numbers into a chart that actually makes the pattern obvious at a glance.
modules.intro: A well-chosen chart can show in one glance what would take paragraphs to describe in words. The trick is matching the chart type to the kind of comparison you're actually making.
core: Use a bar chart to compare a handful of categories, a line chart to show change over time, and a scatter plot to look for a relationship between two numeric variables.
Every chart should be labeled: axis titles with units, a legend if there's more than one series, and a clear title stating what the chart shows.
Sorting bars by value (instead of alphabetically) usually makes a comparison easier to read at a glance.
More color or decoration doesn't make a chart more informative — it often hides the pattern you're trying to show.
modules.example:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
df.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum().plot(kind="bar")
plt.ylabel("Revenue ($)")
plt.title("Revenue by Region")
plt.show()
modules.exercise: Using the dataset from the pandas module, make one bar chart and one line chart (if you have any date-like column) with proper axis labels and a title.

links.title: From Data to Viz — chart chooser

modules.title: Statistics Primer
modules.body: Mean, median, spread, and correlation — the handful of ideas that most data questions come back to.
modules.intro: You don't need advanced math to ask good questions of data — a small set of statistical ideas covers most everyday cases.
core: The mean (average) is sensitive to outliers; the median (the middle value) is not. When a dataset has extreme values, the median often tells a truer story.
Spread — variance and standard deviation — tells you how reliable an average actually is. Two datasets can have the same mean and look completely different once you account for spread.
Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together, from -1 to 1, but a strong correlation never proves that one variable causes the other.
A classic example: ice cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in summer — they're correlated, but neither causes the other; both are driven by warm weather.
modules.example:
import pandas as pd
print(df["revenue"].mean(), df["revenue"].median())
print(df[["revenue", "marketing_spend"]].corr())
modules.exercise: Take any two numeric columns in a dataset you have access to and compute their correlation. Write one sentence about what a confounding factor might be if the correlation turns out to be strong.

modules.title: Intro to Machine Learning
modules.body: Train a simple model on your cleaned data and see what it gets right, and where it doesn't.
modules.intro: Machine learning, at its simplest, is teaching a program to find a pattern in examples so it can make predictions on new, unseen data.
core: Features are the inputs a model learns from (e.g. square footage, number of bedrooms); the label is what it's trying to predict (e.g. house price).
A train/test split holds back some data the model never sees during training, so you can honestly check whether it generalizes rather than just memorizing.
scikit-learn's pattern is consistent across models: model.fit(X_train, y_train) to train, model.predict(X_test) to get predictions.
Accuracy alone can be misleading — a model that always predicts "no" can score 95% accuracy on data where only 5% of cases are "yes", while being useless.
modules.example:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.score(X_test, y_test))
modules.exercise: Using scikit-learn's built-in sample datasets (e.g. sklearn.datasets.load_diabetes), split the data, train a simple regression model, and print its score on the held-out test set.

title: UI/UX Design Principles
description: Learn to think like a designer: understand the user first, then sketch, test, and refine the interface.

modules.title: Design Thinking
modules.body: Start from the person using the product, not the feature list — frame problems before you sketch solutions.
modules.intro: Design thinking is a way of working that puts the person using a product ahead of the features on a spec sheet. It's less a rigid process than a habit of checking your assumptions against real people before committing to a solution.
core: The five commonly cited stages are: empathize (understand the user's real situation), define (frame the actual problem), ideate (generate many possible solutions), prototype (make a rough version), and test (see how real people respond).
A well-framed problem statement focuses on the user's need, not a specific solution — "commuters need to know when the next bus arrives" rather than "we need an app."
The stages aren't strictly linear — testing often sends you back to redefine the problem once you see how people actually behave.
Cheap, early prototypes (paper, sketches) are meant to be thrown away; that's what makes them useful for testing ideas fast.
modules.exercise: Pick an everyday frustration (e.g. finding parking, splitting a bill with friends). Write a one-sentence problem statement focused on the user's need, not a solution, then list three completely different ways you might solve it.

links.title: Interaction Design Foundation — What is Design Thinking?

modules.title: Color & Typography
modules.body: Build a small, deliberate palette and type scale, and learn why most screens need fewer choices, not more.
modules.intro: Color and type are the two elements a person notices before reading a single word — and both work best when constrained to a small, deliberate set of choices rather than picked ad hoc, screen by screen.
core: A simple palette often follows a 60-30-10 split: a dominant neutral (60%), a secondary color (30%), and an accent used sparingly for emphasis (10%).
A type scale — a small set of font sizes, like 14/16/20/28/40px — keeps headings and body text consistent across every screen instead of being picked freely each time.
Contrast isn't just aesthetic: WCAG accessibility guidelines require a minimum contrast ratio (commonly 4.5:1 for body text) so text stays legible for people with low vision.
Limiting yourself to one or two typefaces (often one for headings, one for body) reads as more intentional than mixing several.
modules.exercise: Pick a dominant color, a secondary color, and one accent color for a hypothetical app. Check the contrast between your text color and background using a free contrast checker, and adjust until it passes.

links.title: Nielsen Norman Group — Typography Terms Every Designer Should Know

modules.title: Wireframing
modules.body: Sketch a screen's structure fast and cheap, before any pixel is final, to test layout ideas quickly.
modules.intro: A wireframe is a rough sketch of a screen's layout — boxes for images, lines for text, no color or final type — meant to test structure before anyone invests time in visual polish.
core: Low fidelity (pencil and paper, or simple boxes) is for testing layout ideas fast and cheap; it invites blunt feedback because nothing looks "finished" yet.
Higher fidelity wireframes add more real structure (actual spacing, real content length) once the rough layout has been validated.
Common elements to block out: navigation, primary content area, calls to action, and any repeating pattern like a card or list item.
It's far cheaper to throw away and redo a five-minute sketch than a fully designed, polished screen.
modules.exercise: On paper or in any drawing tool, sketch three different layout ideas for a single screen (e.g. a recipe app's main page) in under five minutes each. Notice how much you can compare once none of them are precious.

modules.title: Prototyping
modules.body: Link static screens into something a person can click through, so a flow can be tested before it's built.
modules.intro: A prototype connects individual screens into something a person can actually click through — which tests a *flow*, not just how one screen looks in isolation.
core: Fidelity should match the question you're asking: a rough clickable sketch is enough to test whether a flow makes sense; a polished, near-final prototype is needed to test visual details.
Linking screens (tapping a button leads to the next screen) surfaces problems a set of static images never would — like a confusing number of steps, or a dead end.
Most modern design tools (Figma, Adobe XD) let you link frames together into a prototype without writing any code.
Test a prototype with a specific task in mind ("find and book a table for two") rather than just asking someone to "look around."
modules.exercise: Using any design tool you have access to (even simple slides work), link three to four screens into a clickable flow for a basic task, like signing up for an account. Try clicking through it yourself as if you were a first-time user.

modules.title: Usability Testing
modules.body: Watch someone use your prototype, notice where they hesitate, and turn that into a short list of fixes.
modules.intro: Usability testing means watching a real person attempt a task on your design and paying attention to what they actually do, not just what they say afterward.
core: Jakob Nielsen's well-known finding is that testing with about five users typically surfaces most major usability problems — you don't need dozens of participants to learn a lot.
The think-aloud protocol asks participants to narrate their thoughts as they work, which surfaces confusion in the moment rather than in a memory-shaped summary afterward.
Give participants a specific, realistic task ("find this product and add it to your cart") instead of an open-ended "explore the site."
Hesitation, backtracking, and re-reading are all signals worth writing down, even if the participant eventually completes the task.
modules.exercise: Ask a friend to complete one specific task using an app or website you use often, while thinking out loud, and just watch — don't help. Write down every moment they hesitated or backtracked.

title: Digital Marketing Essentials
description: Understand how people find and choose a product online, from search to social to the numbers behind it.

modules.title: Marketing Fundamentals
modules.body: The basic shape of a marketing funnel, and where each channel you'll learn next fits into it.
modules.intro: Most marketing activity can be mapped onto a funnel: a large number of people become aware of a product, a smaller number consider it seriously, and a smaller number still actually decide to buy.
core: Awareness stage: people encounter your brand for the first time — social posts, search ads, and word of mouth typically live here.
Consideration stage: people are comparing options — content like comparison guides, reviews, and case studies matters most here.
Decision stage: people are ready to act — clear pricing, testimonials, and a low-friction checkout matter most here.
Not every channel needs to do every job: a search ad usually targets people already close to a decision, while a broad social campaign often targets pure awareness.
modules.exercise: Pick a product you've bought recently. Write down one specific piece of marketing (an ad, a post, a review) that influenced you at each stage of the funnel — awareness, consideration, decision.

links.title: HubSpot — What Is a Marketing Funnel?
Google Digital Garage — Fundamentals of Digital Marketing

modules.title: SEO Basics
modules.body: Help a page show up in search results by understanding what search engines are actually looking for.
modules.intro: Search engine optimization is about helping a page rank well for the searches its intended audience is actually typing in — which means starting from how people search, not just what you want to say.
core: Keyword research means finding the actual words and phrases people search, which are often more specific and more informal than the terms a business would use internally.
On-page factors — a clear title tag, a descriptive meta description, headings that use relevant terms naturally — help search engines understand what a page is about.
Technical factors matter too: page load speed and mobile-friendliness both affect ranking, independent of the content itself.
Backlinks (other sites linking to yours) act as a trust signal — search engines treat them roughly like word-of-mouth recommendations.
modules.exercise: Pick a product or service and write three different search queries a real customer might type when looking for it. Search each one yourself and notice how differently the results are worded — that gap often reveals a content opportunity.

modules.title: Social Media Strategy
modules.body: Pick the right platform for an audience and plan content that earns attention instead of interrupting it.
modules.intro: A social media strategy starts with matching a platform to where your actual audience already spends time and what kind of content they go there expecting — not posting the same thing everywhere.
core: Different platforms have different norms: short-form video, professional networking, visual inspiration — posting content that fights the platform's format usually underperforms.
A content calendar, planned even loosely a few weeks ahead, tends to beat sporadic high-effort posts because consistency builds an audience that returns.
Engagement (likes, comments, shares) is a means to an end — it feeds the platform's algorithm and builds trust, but it isn't the actual business goal.
It's usually better to do one or two platforms well than to spread thin attempting a presence everywhere.
modules.exercise: Pick one platform your target audience uses. Sketch a two-week content calendar (just titles/topics, not full posts) that mixes at least three different content types (e.g. tips, behind-the-scenes, customer stories).

modules.title: Content Creation
modules.body: Write and shape content that holds attention, from a headline through to a clear call to action.
modules.intro: Good marketing content earns attention rather than demanding it — which comes down to specific, concrete writing more than clever phrasing.
core: A headline's only job is to earn the next sentence — it doesn't need to say everything, just enough to make someone want to keep reading.
Every piece of content should point toward one clear next action (read more, sign up, reply) rather than several competing ones.
Specific, concrete claims ("loads in under one second") are more persuasive and more memorable than vague ones ("lightning-fast").
Editing for length usually helps more than editing for cleverness — cutting unnecessary words keeps the reader's attention on what matters.
modules.exercise: Take a piece of marketing copy you've written or seen with a vague claim ("great customer service", "high quality") and rewrite it as one specific, concrete claim instead.

links.title: CoSchedule — How to Write a Blog Post

modules.title: Analytics & Metrics
modules.body: Read a dashboard without getting lost — which numbers actually tell you if something is working.
modules.intro: A marketing dashboard can show dozens of numbers at once — the skill isn't knowing all of them, it's knowing which ones actually connect to a decision you're able to make.
core: A vanity metric looks impressive (total page views, follower count) but rarely changes what you'd do next; an actionable metric is tied to a specific decision.
Conversion rate — the percentage of visitors who complete a goal — often matters more than raw traffic, since more visitors who don't convert isn't actually progress.
Metrics only mean something compared against a baseline or a goal — "1,000 visitors" is meaningless without knowing what last month, or your target, looked like.
A spike in traffic isn't automatically good news — it matters where it came from and whether those visitors did anything once they arrived.
modules.exercise: Look at any analytics dashboard you have access to (a website, a social account). Pick one vanity metric and one actionable metric you can see, and write one sentence on what decision the actionable metric could actually inform.

links.title: CXL — Actionable Metrics vs. Vanity Metrics
